text:
Jim Cramer’s 25 Investing Rules Global Stocks Drift as Trade Tensions, Emerging Market Weakness, Hit Sentiment Global stocks drifted lower Monday as investors continue to worry that the escalating trade war between the Washington and Beijing will damage the world economy as the White House prepares to slap a new set of tariffs on imports from China. Sep3,20185:15AMEDT London Stock Exchange The Monday Market Minute Global stocks drift lower as U.S.-China trade tensions, emerging market currency weakness keeps bulls from taking control. European stocks open softer as investors eye softening PMI data from China and prep for a new set of U.S. tariffs on $200 billion worth of China-made goods. Britain's FTSE 100 gains as pound falls below 1.3 after the EU's chief negotiator trashes Prime Minster Theresa May's Brexit proposal. Market Snapshot
Global stocks drifted lower Monday, with European markets following on from weakness in Asia, as investors continue to worry that the escalating trade war between the Washington and Beijing will damage the world economy as the White House prepares to slap a new set of tariffs on imports from China.
The ongoing weakness in emerging market currencies was also a factor in muting any attempt to take the recent gains from U.S. stocks into markets around the world, as the strong dollar continues to pressure countries high levels of foreign currency debt.
Against that backdrop, markets in Asia were notably weaker across the board Monday, with the MSCI ex-Japan index falling 0.66% and Japan's Nikkei 225 closing 0.7% lower at 22,707.38 points. China stocks were on the back foot once again, with the Shanghahi Composite and the CSI 300 falling 0.2% and 0.4% respectively amid private sector data that showed manufacturing activity -- and crucially new export orders -- coming in at the slowest pace in 14 months in August.
The reading adds further fuel to concerns that China's economy will slow even more quickly than expected in the final months of the year as the impact of President Donald Trump's trade tariffs bite, particularly given the fact that a fresh set of 25% levies on $200 billion worth of goods is likely to be unveiled as early as Thursday.
The prospect for slower growth in the world's second largest economy -- not to mention the world's biggest consumer of energy and basic resources -- kept European stocks in the red Monday even as volumes remained thin owing to today's Labor Day holiday in the United States.
The region wide Stoxx Europe 600 index was marked 0.2% lower in the opening hour of trading, with similar percentage declines seen in benchmarks in France and Germany.
Britain's FTSE 100 was the region's outlier, however, with the index rising 0.67% as the pound retreated to 1.2890 against the dollar following comments from the EU chief Brexit negotiator, Michel Barnier, which comprehensively dismissed Prime Minister Theresa May's so-called 'Chequers Plan' for withdraw from the bloc.
The currency was also hit by PMI data that showed manufacturing activity slowed to its weakest pace in more than two years last month as the impact of Brexit uncertainty hammered inward investment. UK Manufacturing PMI at 52.8 in August, lowest since the immediate aftermath of the #Brexit vote. Exports falling at the steepest pace since October 2014 despite weak #GBP . Output indicates stagnant production https://t.co/MCOX7Fxpl6 pic.twitter.com/koZdH3hW1w — Chris Williamson (@WilliamsonChris) September 3, 2018
The global moves represent a stark contrast to gains in U.S. stocks, where a roaring economy helped the S&P 500 ^GSPC gain 6.7% over what is traditionally the worst month of the year for domestic markets. The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite fared even better, rising just under thanks in part to a 23% surge for Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) , which took the world's biggest company to a series of all-time highs that now value the group at 1.1 trillion. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained just over 7% during the month of August.
Emerging market currency weakness added to the broader market pessimism, as well, as the U.S. dollar index traded near a two-week high of 95.06 against basket of its global peers. The gains, alongside concerns that the $3.7 trillion in dollar-denominated debts taken on by emerging market economies since the global financial crisis is growing increasingly more difficult to maintain, helped push the Indonesian rupiah to a two-decade low of 14,777 against the dollar.
Turkey's lira, too, resumed its decline, falling a further 2% from Friday's modest rally to change hands at 6.69 against the dollar after data showed August inflation surged to 17.9%. Still, Finance Minister Berat Albayrak told Reuters that there is not risk to either the country's banks or its external debts, $180 billion of which comes due next year.
Global oil prices were modestly higher in early European trading, with investors once again balancing reports of a rise in OPEC production, as well as near-record output from the United States, against the looming sanctions on the sale of Iranian crude and the ongoing supply disruptions from crisis-torn Venezuela.
Brent crude contracts for November delivery were marked 23 cents higher from their Friday close in New York and changing hands at $77.90 per barrel while WTI contracts for the same month were seen just a few cents higher at $69.43 per barrel.
